content.text:
Restatement

We are given a rectangular “base” and N non-overlapping sensors, each a circle of radius r_i centered at (x_i, y_i), strictly inside the rectangle. Allen starts at S = (x_s, y_s) and wants to reach T = (x_t, y_t) by running along straight segments, possibly changing direction at intermediate waypoints P = {p1, p2, …}. His polyline must:
- Lie inside the rectangle (running along the border is allowed).
- Never enter the interior of any circle (touching the circle boundary is allowed because detection is strictly “inside”).
- Use at most 1000 turning points.

We must output any feasible set P.

Key observations

1) Existence: The circles are strictly inside the rectangle and pairwise disjoint (distance between centers > r_i + r_j). The free space (rectangle minus open disks) is path-connected, so a feasible path always exists.

2) Convexity of the rectangle: If both endpoints of a segment are inside the rectangle, the entire segment stays inside. Therefore, it suffices to ensure that all chosen points lie in the rectangle; then every straight segment between them will also lie in the rectangle.

3) “Safe” straight lines and tangency: A line tangent to a circle touches it at one point and leaves the disk entirely on one side of the line. Thus, from a tangency point A on the circle, any segment going into the “outer” half-plane (the half-plane not containing the disk) is automatically safe with respect to that circle. This is extremely useful for building safe long segments once you are at a tangency point.

4) Visibility graph with tangencies: For motion among disjoint convex obstacles (circles), a shortest (piecewise straight) path, if you restrict to straight segments only, uses tangency points and “free” bitangents (line segments tangent to two obstacles). Building a graph from all such tangency events and connecting them by collision-free straight segments will contain a feasible path (and even the shortest one). We do not need the shortest path, but exploiting this structure gives a robust construction that always finds a valid path if one exists.

High-level plan

Build a graph whose vertices are “important” points on the boundary of the circles (tangency points) and the endpoints S, T and the rectangle’s four corners. Add straight-line edges only when the segment is guaranteed to be outside all disks. Then run a shortest path (or any) graph search from S to T. The sequence of internal vertices found is the requested set P.

What goes into the graph

Vertices:
- S (start), T (target).
- The four rectangle corners: (xL, yL), (xL, yR), (xR, yL), (xR, yR). These serve as “far away” anchor points. Although you cannot always move along the rectangle edges safely (you still must avoid circles), corners are very useful because many directions from a tangency point to a corner are “away from” the circle.
- All circle-to-circle bitangent touch points:
  For every unordered pair of circles (i, j), there are 4 common tangents: two outer tangents and two inner tangents. For each tangent line, we get a tangency point on circle i and another on circle j. Add both points as vertices (and the segment between them as a candidate edge; see below).
- All point-to-circle tangency points:
  For each circle i, compute the two tangency points from S to circle i and the two tangency points from T to circle i. Add these as vertices.

Candidate edges (straight segments) and when to keep them:
- S ↔ T: add if the direct segment is safe (does not enter any disk interior).
- S ↔ each of its two tangency points on circle i: add if that segment is safe with respect to all other circles (it is automatically safe with respect to circle i by construction).
- T ↔ each of its two tangency points similarly.
- Between the two endpoints of every circle-to-circle bitangent: add the segment if it stays outside all other circles. It is automatically safe with respect to the two touched circles.
- From a tangency point A on any circle to a rectangle corner R if R lies in the “outer half-plane” of the tangent line at A. This guarantees safety with respect to that circle; keep the edge only if it is also safe with respect to all other circles. (How to test outer half-plane is explained below.)
- Optionally, you may also attempt edges S/corners/T pairwise and keep only the safe ones. This just gives the search more options, it is not required for correctness.

How to compute the geometric primitives

All computations can be done in doubles with a small ε (e.g., 1e-9 to 1e-8) to guard against floating-point roundoff. The judge uses ε = 1e-6.

A) Distance from a segment to a circle
- Given segment PQ and circle center C with radius r:
  - Let d = Q − P, w = C − P.
  - Project: t0 = clamp( dot(w, d) / |d|^2, 0, 1 ).
  - Closest point on the segment: X = P + t0 d.
  - Distance: dist = |C − X|.
  - The segment is safe w.r.t. this circle if dist ≥ r − eps. Use a small eps like 1e-9 so that true tangency is accepted.

B) Tangents between two circles (bitangents)
Let circle i: center Ci, radius ri; circle j: center Cj, radius rj; vector u = (Cj − Ci), d = |u|. Because d > ri + rj, all four bitangents exist.
- Build an orthonormal basis: û = u / d, v̂ = perp(û) = (−û_y, û_x).
- We handle two “types” s ∈ {+1, −1}:
  - s = +1 for outer tangents,
  - s = −1 for inner tangents.
  Define rj' = s ⋅ rj and h = (ri − rj') / d. By the input guarantee, |h| < 1.
- For each sign t ∈ {+1, −1} (the two mirror solutions):
  - Let n = −h ⋅ û + t ⋅ sqrt(1 − h^2) ⋅ v̂. This is a unit normal to the tangent line.
  - Tangency points:
    - Ti = Ci + ri ⋅ n
    - Tj = Cj + rj' ⋅ n  (note: if s = −1 then rj' = −rj, so this subtracts)
  - Candidate edge is segment Ti–Tj. It is tangent to both circles and safe w.r.t. them; keep it only if it is also safe w.r.t. all other circles.

C) Tangents from a point P to a circle
Let circle: center C, radius r; vector u = P − C, d = |u| (> r is guaranteed). Let û = u / d and v̂ = perp(û).
- Let h = r / d and t = sqrt(1 − h^2).
- There are two unit normals:
  - n1 = h ⋅ û + t ⋅ v̂
  - n2 = h ⋅ û − t ⋅ v̂
- Tangency points:
  - T1 = C + r ⋅ n1
  - T2 = C + r ⋅ n2
- Candidate edges P–T1 and P–T2. They are tangent to this circle, but must be checked against other circles.

D) Which rectangle corners are “outside” a tangent line
At a tangency point A = C + r ⋅ n, the tangent line has unit normal n and passes through A. The whole disk lies in the closed half-plane H_in = {X | dot(n, X) ≤ dot(n, A)}. The complementary closed half-plane H_out = {X | dot(n, X) ≥ dot(n, A)} is the safe side.
- A rectangle corner R is “outside” for this tangency if dot(n, R) ≥ dot(n, A) − eps. Then segment A–R is guaranteed safe with respect to this circle (check other circles as usual).

Graph search and output
- After building the nodes and adding all candidate edges that pass the collision checks, run Dijkstra (or any shortest path algorithm) from S to T, using Euclidean lengths as edge weights. A plain BFS would also find a feasible path but not necessarily short; Dijkstra gives a tidy path with few turns.
- The resulting path is a sequence Q = (S = q0, q1, …, qk, q_{k+1} = T). Output |P| = k and the k intermediate points q1 … qk.
- Ensure all points are distinct (drop any consecutive duplicates if numerical coincidence occurs).

Why this works

- The free space (rectangle minus open disks) is connected, so a feasible path exists.

- Geometry of tangencies:
  - For any circle, a straight line tangent at A leaves the disk entirely on one side. Therefore, from A, any segment into the exterior half-plane is guaranteed safe with respect to that circle. Connecting tangency points to suitable rectangle corners leverages this to “escape” away from a circle without hugging it.
  - Between two circles, the common bitangents are exactly the straight lines that are simultaneously supporting to both disks. When the segment between their tangency points is unobstructed by other disks (“free bitangent”), it is an ideal way to thread between obstacles.

- Completeness intuition:
  - It is a standard result in computational geometry that among disjoint convex obstacles, a shortest obstacle-avoiding straight-segment path touches obstacles at tangency points and runs along free bitangents and tangents from start/goal. Our graph contains all of these features (circle–circle bitangents and point–circle tangents), hence contains at least one feasible S–T path.
  - Adding edges from tangency points to rectangle corners strengthens connectivity and covers small-N edge cases (e.g., with a single circle) by providing “far” safe targets in the correct half-plane.

- Rectangle constraints are automatically satisfied because every vertex we use lies inside the rectangle (circles are strictly inside, S and T are strictly inside, corners are on the boundary), and a convex set contains each segment connecting two of its points.

Handling numerical issues
- Use doubles and an epsilon eps ≈ 1e-9 when testing:
  - Segment–circle safety: allow dist ≥ r − eps.
  - Half-plane test for corner connection: dot(n, R) ≥ dot(n, A) − eps.
  - Clamp values inside [-1, 1] before sqrt(1 − h^2).
- Drop edges of near-zero length or nodes that are numerically equal (within eps).
- Print coordinates with sufficient precision (e.g., 10–12 digits after the decimal point).

Pseudocode sketch

- Build inputs: S, T, rectangle [xL, xR] × [yL, yR], circles {Ci, ri}.

- If isFreeSegment(S, T): print 0 and stop.

- V = [S, T, corners]; E = empty.

- For each circle i:
  - Tangents from S: compute T1, T2 with normals n1, n2; add nodes; add edge (S, Tj) if isFreeSegment(S, Tj).
  - Connect each Tj to every corner R that satisfies dot(nj, R) ≥ dot(nj, Tj) − eps and isFreeSegment(Tj, R).
  - Do the same from T.

- For each unordered pair of circles (i, j):
  - For s in {+1, −1}, for t in {+1, −1}:
    - Compute unit normal n; tangency points Ti on circle i and Tj on circle j.
    - Add nodes Ti, Tj (get their ids).
    - If isFreeSegment(Ti, Tj) against all circles: add edge (Ti, Tj).

- Optionally try direct edges among corners, and S/T ↔ corners, keeping only safe ones.

- Run Dijkstra from S to T on (V, E).

- Reconstruct the path Q. Let P be Q without the endpoints (S and T). Output |P| and the points.

Correctness argument
- Safety: Every edge added is checked against all circles; thus every segment lies in free space. All vertices lie inside the rectangle, so the entire polyline stays in the rectangle due to convexity. Tangent endpoints on the circles are allowed because detection is “strictly inside.”
- Existence in the graph: The classic visibility/bitangent graph for convex disjoint obstacles contains a shortest feasible path. Our vertex set includes the exact tangency events needed (circle–circle bitangents; point–circle tangents), and edges include all free bitangents and all safe tangents. Therefore the graph has an S–T path. The corner connections give additional redundancy and help in small or degenerate configurations.
- Output bound: The found path typically uses few segments; with N ≤ 50 the number of turns is far below 1000.

Complexity
- Number of circle pairs: O(N^2) ≤ 1225 for N = 50.
- Per pair, we generate up to 4 bitangents (8 endpoints). Collision-checking an edge costs O(N) circle tests.
- Total edge checks O(N^3) in the low millions of primitive operations, easily within 1 second.
- Dijkstra over O(N^2) vertices and edges is fast (well under 1 ms in typical implementations).

Common pitfalls
- Forgetting that you cannot “follow” a circle boundary with a curved arc: the trajectory must be straight segments only. This is why we use tangency points and straight “free” bitangents, not arcs.
- Not allowing equality in the distance test: touching the circle boundary is permitted. Use a small negative tolerance in your “outside” test to accept true tangencies.
- Numerical issues in sqrt(1 − h^2) when h is very close to ±1. Clamp h to [-1, 1] first.

Summary

- Build a “tangent graph”:
  - Nodes: S, T, corners, all point–circle tangency points, all endpoints of circle–circle bitangents.
  - Edges: keep only straight segments that are safe with respect to all circles. Specifically include all free circle–circle bitangents, S/T to their tangency points, and tangency points to corners in the correct half-plane.
- Run a shortest path on this graph and output the intermediate vertices as P.
- This yields a valid piecewise-linear path that never enters any sensor disk, stays inside the rectangle, and uses far fewer than 1000 turning points.
